strengths: Develops a comprehensive and technically rigorous DMFT-based theory of transfer learning in infinite-width, feature-learning (mu-P/mean-field) neural networks, extending prior single-task feature-learning theories to the two-stage (pretrain/fine-tune or jointly rich) setting.

Provides closed-form, interpretable results in tractable special cases (linear networks, population vs. finite source data, ultra-rich pretraining) that cleanly explain when transfer learning helps or hurts as a function of data amounts (P1, P2), source/target alignment, and feature-learning strength (gamma1, gamma2).

Strong agreement between theoretical DMFT predictions and numerical simulations of finite-but-wide networks (both synthetic polynomial tasks and real datasets such as CIFAR-10), across multiple figures, lending credibility to the theory.

Careful and thorough derivations (path-integral/DMFT for both gradient-flow and Bayesian posterior settings) are included in extensive appendices, making the work reproducible in principle and mathematically self-contained (including a helpful DMFT primer).

Good positioning relative to a large and relevant body of related work (Bayesian transfer learning, NTK/proportional-limit theories, continual learning), with explicit discussion of how this work's mu-P treatment differs from and extends prior Bayesian NTK-based transfer-learning theories.

Identifies non-trivial, somewhat counter-intuitive phenomena (e.g., negative transfer from finite-sample noise, harm from ultra-rich pretraining, asymmetry between easy-to-hard vs hard-to-easy curricula) that are of practical interest beyond the toy models.
weaknesses: The exactly-solvable results are largely restricted to two-layer (shallow) linear or simple nonlinear networks with isotropic Gaussian data; deeper networks are acknowledged to have non-Markovian dynamics that are not solved, and the isotropic-data assumption limits applicability to realistic structured data.

For the finite-data fine-tuning result (Result 3) and its nonlinear/real-data extension, the key constants (c1, c2, c3) are not derived in closed form but left as free parameters, with only an ad hoc large-gamma1 ansatz used to compare against real datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10), weakening the rigor of the empirical validation in the most practically relevant regime.

Real-data experiments are limited in scope (two-layer ReLU MLPs on small binary-class subsets of CIFAR-10, N=20000, relatively small P1/P2), so it is unclear how well the qualitative conclusions generalize to deeper architectures, multi-class settings, or larger-scale data regimes typical of modern transfer learning.

The paper is extremely dense with heavy notation and lengthy derivations (much of the technical content relegated to a very long appendix), which may hinder accessibility and independent verification by non-specialist readers.

While the theory yields many qualitative phase-diagram-type conclusions, some practically important quantities (e.g., precise conditions for the sign of crosstalk/noise effects in general alignment settings) are only worked out in special cases (e.g., alpha_s=1, alpha_g=0), limiting the immediate practical predictive power of the theory.

strengths: Presents a genuinely novel theoretical framework for transfer learning in infinite-width, feature-learning (mean-field/µP) two-layer neural networks, extending beyond prior NTK/proportional-limit theories that either lack feature learning or require Gaussian-equivalence assumptions.

Develops two complementary and mutually consistent formalisms (a Bayesian/replica-based theory and a DMFT gradient-flow theory), both leading to adaptive kernel predictors that explicitly depend on source and target task statistics via an elastic coupling parameter δ.

Careful and thorough positioning relative to closely related prior work (e.g., Ingrosso et al., Shan et al., Tahir et al.), clearly articulating what is technically new (non-Gaussian, non-perturbative kernel adaptation even in the P=Θ(N) regime).

Strong empirical validation: theory predictions (dashed lines) closely match simulations (solid lines) from Langevin dynamics and gradient descent across many settings (linear regression, polynomial/Hermite teacher tasks, CIFAR-10/Fashion-MNIST/MNIST classification, and a CNN extension in the appendix).

Rich and intuitive phenomenology is uncovered and explained: interplay between elastic coupling, feature-learning richness (γ0), task similarity, and target dataset size, including interesting non-monotonic/asymmetric effects when transferring from lower-to-higher or higher-to-lower complexity tasks.
Detailed and self-contained appendix derivations (replica computation, saddle-point equations, DMFT field equations) supporting reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: The theory and most experiments are restricted to two-layer networks; the paper does not address how these results extend to deep networks, which limits direct relevance to practical transfer learning settings where deep architectures dominate.

Real-data experiments are relatively small-scale and simplified (binary class-pair problems on CIFAR-10/Fashion-MNIST/MNIST with very small target sample sizes and grayscale/downsampled inputs), so it is unclear how well the theory's qualitative predictions would generalize to realistic transfer-learning workloads or modern architectures (e.g., ResNets, transformers).

The theory does not average over the data distribution (acknowledged explicitly as a limitation), so the resulting equations scale with the number of datapoints and do not yield clean closed-form predictions for generalization as a function of P2 and task alignment in the way some prior spectral-bias theories do.

Some qualitative explanations (e.g., the grokking-like conjecture behind the high-to-low degree polynomial transfer results in Fig. 5) are offered somewhat speculatively without rigorous theoretical support beyond intuition.

The connection to practical fine-tuning methods (e.g., low-rank adaptation such as LoRA) is only briefly discussed as future work despite being highly relevant to current transfer-learning practice, somewhat limiting the paper's practical significance.

The presentation is extremely dense and notation-heavy, which may limit accessibility to a broader ML audience outside the statistical-mechanics/mean-field theory community; the main text often relies heavily on appendix derivations for full understanding.
